claims.claim: Media ownership is concentrated: in the United States, a small number of large corporations control a large share of major media outlets, a structure commonly described as an oligopoly.

Concentration has increased over time through mergers and consolidation; radio ownership consolidated heavily from the 1990s onward as large radio groups bought many local stations, and newspaper chains have long owned papers across many markets.

Vertical integration means one company owns multiple stages of the same industry, such as producing content and also owning the channels or delivery systems that distribute it; the Comcast-NBC Universal combination is a widely cited media example.

Horizontal integration (horizontal concentration) means a company expands within the same media sector by acquiring more outlets of the same kind, such as a radio company buying many local radio stations.

The FCC, created by the Communications Act of 1934, licenses broadcast stations and administers ownership rules that limit how many stations one company can own nationally and within local markets; its stated policy goals include competition, localism, and diversity.

FCC ownership rules have been relaxed over time: deregulation accelerated in the 1980s, the 1996 Telecommunications Act relaxed limits and required periodic FCC review of the ownership rules, and in 2017 the FCC eliminated the newspaper/broadcast cross-ownership rule and the radio/television cross-ownership rule while retaining other limits.

The debate over consolidation is live and attributed: critics argue that concentration reduces the diversity of voices and information and threatens independent media and accountability, while supporters of deregulation argue that regulations harm consumers and that common ownership creates efficiencies such as shared newsgathering resources.

Media outlets fund themselves mainly from consumers (sales and subscriptions), advertising, or public and nonprofit support; because revenue sources shape what content is produced, asking who owns and who pays for an outlet is a core media-literacy question.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether ownership concentration helps or harms the media landscape
positions: Critics argue that consolidation reduces the diversity of voices and information and weakens the accountability of media owners to the public; Robert McChesney links concentration to deregulation, and a 2003 OSCE report by Johannes von Dohnanyi warns that horizontal concentration may endanger media pluralism while vertical concentration may create entry barriers for new competitors (positions as summarized in the Wikipedia survey).

Supporters of deregulation argue that ownership limits and other regulations harm consumers and that large combined companies create efficiencies; the FCC itself credited this view in its 2017 order, observing that newspaper/broadcast combinations can promote localism by sharing expertise, resources, and capital, which can raise the quantity and quality of local news.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both positions as attributed views in an ongoing policy debate (the FCC reviews the rules periodically) and does not adjudicate between them.

sourceRecords.title: 2014 Quadrennial Regulatory Review (Order on Reconsideration, FCC 17-156, 83 FR 733)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the Federal Register edition on federalregister.gov (official edition on govinfo, 83 FR 733; adopted by the FCC November 16, 2017). Supports: the FCC's periodic review of its broadcast ownership rules under Section 202(h) of the Telecommunications Act of 1996; the repeal of the Newspaper/Broadcast Cross-Ownership Rule (adopted 1975) and the Radio/Television Cross-Ownership Rule; revision of the Local Television Ownership Rule (Eight-Voices Test eliminated, Top-Four Prohibition retained in modified form); retention of the Local Radio Ownership Rule; the FCC's competition, localism, and diversity policy goals; and the FCC's finding that newspaper/broadcast combinations can promote localism through shared expertise, resources, and capital. Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Concentration of media ownership
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Tier D secondary survey used for attributed positions and general definitions only: concentration defined as fewer individuals or organizations controlling shares of the mass media; the U.S. landscape described as an oligopoly (citing Straubhaar, LaRose, and Davenport); horizontal concentration defined as concentration of media ownership within a given media sector; vertical concentration defined as integration of the different phases of production and distribution; radio consolidation following the Telecommunications Act of 1996 (iHeartMedia/Clear Channel example); McChesney's deregulation argument and the opposing view that regulations harm consumers; critics' concerns about reduced diversity of information and accountability; and von Dohnanyi's 2003 OSCE report on pluralism and entry barriers. General claims kept deliberately general; no specific statistics from this source were reproduced in the lesson.
